title: A Company Lives Where It Is Run, and Work Can Be Taxed Where It Happens
summary: Where a company is resident for tax is often decided by where it is really managed, not only where it was formed. A business can also be taxed in a country where it has no company at all, if it has a permanent establishment there. This lesson explains both ideas and the one habit that protects you: a substance record kept as you go.
body:
A company is not resident where its certificate was printed. In many systems it is resident where its real decisions are made, and its work can be taxed where it is done. Both questions are answered by evidence, so keep the evidence as you go.

Recall

Q. What is a share pledge?

A. Security over the shares of a company, which lets a lender take control of the company if the loan defaults.

Q. What are the four steps of the owner's control loop?

A. Plan, with a charter and frozen baseline; measure, with monthly earned value; decide, through change control at the right authority; and record, in the owner decision log.

Q. What does a project charter contain?

A. The project's purpose, the owner's representative, the approval authorities and the reporting cadence, written down before work starts.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week Omar showed that a holding company in another country can save real money, but only if it qualifies, and that qualification usually depends on residence and substance. This week is about that dependency. A structure that looks perfect on paper can be taxed as if it lived somewhere else, because of where emails were sent from, who really decided and where the work happened. Ford joins me on Day 2 with a case where exactly that happened. These are concepts; every country defines residence and taxable presence in its own law and treaties, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Where a company lives

In plain English: a country may treat a company as its own resident because it was formed there, or because it is really run from there, or both.

The professional framing gives two broad tests. The incorporation test treats a company as resident where it was incorporated. The management test treats it as resident where its central management and control is exercised: where the high-level strategic decisions are actually made, typically by its board. The management test has deep roots in the common law; a British case from 1906, De Beers Consolidated Mines against Howe, held a company registered in South Africa to be resident in the United Kingdom because its board in London controlled it. Many common law countries apply some version of both tests, so a company can be resident in two countries at once, which treaties try to resolve and Week 57 covers.

A worked example, hypothetical. You form a holding company in Country B. Its two directors live in Country B. Each quarter they receive a board pack, but the decisions in it, which projects to fund, what dividends to pay, whom to lend to, are settled by you in calls and emails from your home in Country A, and the directors sign what you send. On a management test, an authority in Country A may conclude the company is managed and controlled where you are, and treat it as resident in Country A. If so, the withholding saving Omar modelled disappears, and the company may also owe tax in Country A on its income.

Taxed where the work happens

In plain English: even without a company in a country, a business can owe tax there if it has a fixed place of business there or someone there habitually concluding contracts for it.

The professional framing is the permanent establishment (PE), a concept defined mainly in tax treaties, many of which follow a model published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Typical forms include an office, branch or workshop; a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts on the business's behalf; and, important for builders, a building site or construction project that lasts longer than a period set in the treaty. The period varies from treaty to treaty; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. If a PE exists, the country where it sits may tax the profit attributable to it.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your development company, resident in Country A, builds a project in Country C and runs it with its own staff on site. The treaty between A and C says a construction site creates a PE if it lasts more than a set number of months. The project takes 20 months from site mobilisation to handover. Unless the treaty threshold is longer than that, Country C may tax the profit attributable to the project, and your pro forma should carry that tax from day one. Splitting one project into short contracts to stay under the threshold is the kind of arrangement many treaties now address expressly.

Say that out loud now.

Residence follows where decisions are made; a permanent establishment follows where the work is done.

The substance record

Both questions are decided on evidence, often years later, by someone who was not there. The protection is a substance record: a file, kept as events happen, showing where and by whom each significant decision was made. It holds the board calendar and attendance, the minutes with the papers the directors actually considered, records of where directors were when they decided, the entity's own office lease, staff and bank mandate, and travel logs for anyone whose presence could create a PE. A good record shows decisions being made, not merely signed. A record assembled after an audit letter arrives is evidence of something else.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: residence and PE decide which country taxes what, and a wrong answer can mean tax in two places. Liability: directors who sign without deciding may face personal exposure for the decisions they approved. Banking: banks ask where an entity is managed for their own compliance, and inconsistent answers raise flags. Governance: the board must really govern, with its own papers, debate and minutes. Estate: a trust or company that is resident where you live may fall into your estate's tax net. Exit: a buyer's diligence will test residence history, and an unresolved exposure reduces the price.

Professional sign-off required: international tax adviser in each country involved.

Why a developer is especially exposed

Developers are more exposed to both questions than most investors, for two reasons. First, development is decision-heavy. A passive holding company that owns one stabilised building makes few decisions a year, so its board can genuinely make them. A company that is buying land, appointing consultants, approving budgets and drawing loans makes dozens of decisions a month, and the person closest to them, usually you, will be tempted to make them directly. Second, construction is physical. A site is a fixed place, staff are present for long periods, and contracts are negotiated and signed locally. That is the fact pattern permanent establishment rules were written for.

So the design answer often separates the two: a holding company that holds and decides a small number of big things where it is resident, and a development or management company that does the daily work where the work is, registered and taxed there, with fees between them set at arm's length. Each entity then lives where its decisions and its work really are, which is the only position that stays true under examination.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an entity that is formed abroad and run from home. The paperwork says one country; the emails say another, and the emails usually win. The control is a written decision protocol: which decisions belong to the board, where it meets, and a rule that you do not instruct the directors on those decisions.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks holding board meetings abroad is enough. A meeting that only approves what was decided elsewhere is a meeting, not management. Authorities look for where the thinking happened.

Callback

In Week 22, Elias taught residence versus source: a resident is usually taxed on worldwide income, a non-resident on income from local sources. This week sharpens both halves. Residence is a question of fact about where control sits, and source can include profit from a permanent establishment you created simply by building there.

Recap

A company may be resident where it was formed, where it is really managed, or both. A business can be taxed where it has a permanent establishment, including a long construction site. Both are decided by evidence, so keep a substance record as you go, and never run a foreign entity from home.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: the Fundy Settlement case, where trusts formed abroad were held to live where they were really run.
checklist: I know whether each of my entities is resident by incorporation, by management or both.
I can name who makes each entity's strategic decisions and where.
I have a written decision protocol for every foreign entity.
I never instruct foreign directors on decisions that belong to their board.
I check the construction PE threshold in any treaty before building abroad.
My pro forma carries foreign tax on any project likely to create a PE.
I keep a substance record as decisions happen, not after.
I keep travel logs for anyone whose presence could create a PE.
head: Field checklist
speak: Where a company is resident for tax can be decided by where it was formed, or by where it is really managed: where the board makes the high-level strategic decisions. A British case from 1906, De Beers, held a South African company resident in London because its board there controlled it, and many countries still apply a management test, so a company can be resident in two places at once. Separately, a business can be taxed in a country where it has no company at all, through a permanent establishment: an office, a dependent agent who concludes contracts, or a construction site lasting longer than the period a treaty sets. Both questions are decided on evidence, years later. So I keep a substance record as I go: board calendars, minutes with real papers, where directors were when they decided, and travel logs. And I never run a foreign entity from home, because the emails usually win.
terms: Central management and control — the place where a company's high-level strategic decisions are actually made, used by some countries to decide residence.
Permanent establishment (PE) — a fixed place of business or dependent agent through which a business becomes taxable in a country under a treaty.
Substance record — a file kept as events happen, showing where and by whom an entity's significant decisions were made.

hostile.q: Your holding company's directors live abroad, but every decision in its minutes matches an email you sent the week before. Where is it really managed?
hostile.a: On those facts, an authority could reasonably say it is managed where I am, and I would not argue otherwise. That is why we now run it differently: the board receives papers with options, not instructions; it meets in its country of residence and its minutes record its own debate; I attend as a shareholder only when invited; and the substance record shows who decided what and where. If I cannot step back from those decisions, I should assume the company is resident where I live and plan for that.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole (audit and integrity) assisting
title: Fundy Settlement 2012: Trusts That Lived Where They Were Really Run
summary: In 2012 the Supreme Court of Canada held that two trusts formed with a trustee in Barbados were resident in Canada, because their central management and control was exercised by beneficiaries in Canada rather than by the trustee. The treaty benefit claimed on a large share sale was lost. The case shows that residence follows real control, whatever the documents say.
body:
In April 2012 the Supreme Court of Canada decided that two trusts with a trustee in Barbados were resident in Canada. The documents said Barbados. The court looked at who really managed the trusts, found it was people in Canada, and the treaty benefit claimed on a large gain was gone.

Recall

Q. What is a permanent establishment?

A. A fixed place of business or a dependent agent through which a business becomes taxable in a country under a treaty, including in many treaties a construction site lasting longer than a set period.

Q. What is the multi-employer doctrine?

A. An OSHA enforcement policy under which more than one employer on a site can be cited for one hazard, depending on who created, was exposed to, was responsible for correcting or controlled it.

Q. What is a work breakdown structure?

A. A numbered tree that splits a project into deliverables, with each element tied to one cost code and one schedule activity.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole assists because this is a tax and evidence case. The decision is Fundy Settlement against Canada, reported as 2012 SCC 14, and the earlier trial decision in the Tax Court of Canada is often cited by the name of the family involved, Garron. The facts below come from the published judgments. I do not quote the amounts at stake, and I describe the planning in general terms. Trust and estate examples later in this lesson are hypothetical.

1. Timeline

In the late 1990s, as part of a reorganisation of a family business in Canada, two trusts were settled with a trust company resident in Barbados as trustee. The trusts acquired shares in Canadian companies. Some years later the shares were sold at a large gain. The trusts claimed that, as residents of Barbados, they were protected from Canadian tax on the gain under the tax treaty between Canada and Barbados. The Canada Revenue Agency assessed them as residents of Canada. The Tax Court agreed with the agency in 2009, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in 2010, and the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed the further appeal in April 2012.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions shaped the result. Choosing a foreign trustee whose role, by agreement, was limited to administration. Leaving the substantive decisions about the trust property, including the decision to sell, with people resident in Canada. And relying on the treaty benefit at the point of sale, when the evidence of who had been managing the trusts for years was already fixed.

3. Assumptions

The planning assumed that a trust is resident where its trustee is resident, which had been the common understanding. The courts held instead that a trust, like a company, is resident where its central management and control is actually exercised. The trustee's residence is usually where that happens, but not when the trustee is in practice carrying out decisions made by others. The assumption that legal form would decide residence was the assumption that failed.

4. Incentives

The treaty benefit was large, and the people who cared most about the outcome were the people in Canada who wanted to keep control of the family's wealth. A trustee with real independence might have made decisions they disliked. Every incentive pointed toward keeping control at home while keeping the trustee abroad, which is precisely the combination the court found decisive.

Say that out loud now.

If I keep the decisions, I keep the residence.

5. Warning signs ignored

The trial court found that the trustee had agreed to play a limited role and had deferred to the Canadian beneficiaries on substantive matters. The evidence included how decisions were made and communicated. Any adviser reviewing the arrangement could have asked a simple question: if the trustee disagreed with the family, whose view would prevail? The honest answer, on the facts found, was the family's.

6. Point of no return

Residence is judged on how the entity was run over time. By the date of the sale, years of conduct had already established where management and control sat. Once the gain was realised, no change in conduct could rewrite that history. The point of no return was not the sale; it was the first year the trustee was allowed to be a signatory rather than a decision-maker.

7. Root cause

Cole's finding: the structure separated legal ownership from real control, placed the ownership abroad and the control at home, and kept no evidence that the foreign trustee ever exercised independent judgment, because it did not. The documents described a Barbados trust. The conduct described a Canadian one. Courts decide residence on conduct.

The developer's translation

A worked example, hypothetical and not your family. A developer sets up a holding company abroad with a corporate services provider as its sole director. The developer negotiates every land purchase, approves every loan and decides every dividend, and the provider signs. Under a management test, the company is at serious risk of being resident where the developer lives. The fix is not better minutes. It is real directors who receive options and analysis, debate them, sometimes say no, and record why.

A second example. A developer wants a foreign entity but also wants to keep the final say. The honest answer is to choose. Either accept that the entity is resident at home and plan the tax on that basis, or give real decision-making to people abroad and accept that they may decide differently from you. Wanting both is the Fundy structure.

Cole's test for any foreign entity

Cole's note. Ask three questions and answer them from documents, not intentions. Who has ever said no to the controlling owner, and where is that recorded? Where were the people who made the last five significant decisions on the day they made them? Who drafted the board papers, and did they contain options or instructions? An entity that cannot answer the first question has not yet been tested, and an authority will assume the worst.

What the courts actually weighed

The judgments repay reading, because they show how a court thinks about residence. The trial judge looked at the trust agreements, at the trustee's own understanding of its role, at how it had been chosen and at how decisions about the trust property had in fact been taken and communicated. The trustee was found to have had a limited role, providing administrative services and deferring to the beneficiaries on matters of substance. The Supreme Court endorsed applying the central management and control test to trusts, drawing on the same reasoning used for companies since De Beers, and agreed that on these facts management and control sat in Canada.

For a developer, the point generalises beyond trusts. Every time a tax benefit depends on an entity being resident somewhere, a court can ask the same three things: what the documents say, what the people involved understood their roles to be, and what they actually did. If the third answer contradicts the first, the third wins. Write your governance so all three say the same thing, and then live by it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is keeping real control while placing legal ownership abroad. The control is to decide honestly where you want the entity to live, and then to place the real decisions, the people and the evidence there, consistently, from the first year.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that choosing a foreign trustee or director settles residence. Choosing them is the start. Letting them decide is what makes it true.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught substance over form, and last week Ford took Enron, where form hid substance in accounts. Fundy is the tax version: the form said Barbados, the substance said Canada, and substance won.

Recap

Two trusts with a Barbados trustee were held resident in Canada in 2012, because their central management and control was exercised by people in Canada, and the treaty benefit claimed on a large gain was lost. Rule 56: an entity I set up abroad is governed there in fact, by people who decide and record their own decisions there; if I keep the decisions, I assume it is resident where I live.

Next: Roman, on The Money: pricing a residence challenge and budgeting for real substance.
checklist: I can say honestly where I want each foreign entity to be resident.
Foreign directors or trustees receive options and analysis, not instructions.
My records show at least one decision where a foreign board exercised its own judgment.
I know where the people making each significant decision were when they made it.
I do not keep the final say over an entity I claim is resident abroad.
If I keep control, I plan tax on the basis that the entity is resident where I live.
My substance record starts in the entity's first year.
head: Field checklist
speak: In April 2012 the Supreme Court of Canada decided Fundy Settlement. Two trusts had been settled with a trust company in Barbados as trustee, acquired shares in Canadian companies, and later sold them at a large gain, claiming treaty protection as Barbados residents. The courts held the trusts were resident in Canada, because central management and control was exercised by people in Canada, with the trustee in a limited, administrative role that deferred to them on substance. The planning assumed a trust lives where its trustee lives. The court looked at conduct, not documents. By the date of the sale, years of conduct had already fixed the answer. The root cause was separating legal ownership from real control, ownership abroad and control at home. My rule is Rule 56: an entity I set up abroad is governed there in fact; if I keep the decisions, I assume it is resident where I live.
terms: Trustee — the person or company that holds legal title to trust property and is responsible for managing it for the beneficiaries.
Treaty benefit — a reduction or exemption of tax available under a tax treaty to a resident of a treaty country.
Conduct evidence — records of how an entity was actually run, which courts weigh above what its documents say.

hostile.q: Your foreign holding company has independent directors, but you are its only shareholder. Who would they ever refuse?
hostile.a: They have refused me, and it is in the minutes. Last year the board declined a loan I proposed to another of my companies until it received an independent valuation, and it set a lower dividend than I asked for to keep a reserve. Their papers contain options and analysis, they meet in their country, and I attend only when invited. If they had never said no, I would assume the company is resident where I live and plan accordingly.

rule: Rule 56: Any entity I set up abroad must be governed there in fact, by directors or trustees who make and record their own decisions in that country without taking instructions from me; if I keep the real decisions, I treat the entity as resident where I live.

title: Pricing a Residence Challenge, and What Real Substance Costs
summary: A residence or permanent establishment challenge is a risk that can be priced like any other: the tax at stake, the probability of losing, interest and penalties, and the cost of defending. Against it sits the cost of real substance. This lesson builds both numbers and shows when substance is cheap insurance and when the structure is not worth it.
body:
A tax position is a risk, and risks have prices. Put the expected cost of a residence challenge beside the yearly cost of real substance, and the decision usually makes itself.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 56?

A. Any entity set up abroad is governed there in fact, by people who make and record their own decisions there without taking instructions; if the owner keeps the real decisions, he treats it as resident where he lives.

Q. What is the optimistic estimate at completion?

A. The budget at completion divided by the cost performance index.

Q. What is scope creep, and what stops it?

A. Gradual growth of scope through unapproved additions; it is stopped by change control, meaning a written request, a priced impact and approval at the right authority before work proceeds.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, lenders and investors increasingly ask about tax risk in a structure, because a reassessment can take cash a project needs for debt service. If you can price the risk and show what you spend to reduce it, the conversation is about management. If you cannot, it is about trust. Every figure below is hypothetical, and tax outcomes, interest and penalties depend on local law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The price of a challenge

In plain English: multiply what you would lose by how likely you are to lose it, then add what the fight would cost.

The professional framing is expected cost. Four components. The tax at stake if the position fails. Interest on that tax from when it should have been paid, since many systems charge it. Penalties, which vary widely and may depend on whether you took reasonable care. And defence cost: advisers, time and management attention, which you pay whether you win or lose. The probability of losing is a judgment, best expressed as a range from your adviser, not a single number.

A worked example, hypothetical round numbers. Your holding company's qualification saves 100,000 dollars a year of withholding on dividends from a project. Over five years that is 500,000 dollars. If the company is found resident at home instead, assume the 500,000 dollars of saved withholding becomes payable, plus interest of about 60,000 dollars, plus a penalty of 10 percent, 50,000 dollars, total 610,000 dollars. Defence costs, assume 80,000 dollars. With weak substance your adviser puts the chance of losing at 50 to 70 percent. Expected cost of losing at 60 percent is 366,000 dollars, plus 80,000 dollars of defence, about 446,000 dollars. The structure was meant to save 500,000 dollars. On weak substance, it is worth about 54,000 dollars, before its own running costs.

Say that out loud now.

Tax at stake, plus interest and penalties, times the chance of losing, plus the cost of the fight: that is what a weak position really costs.

The cost of real substance

Now price the alternative. Real substance means the entity can genuinely decide where it claims to live. Hypothetical annual costs: two experienced resident directors at 20,000 dollars each, 40,000 dollars; a small office or shared serviced space, 15,000 dollars; a part-time resident manager who prepares board papers, 30,000 dollars; travel for quarterly in-person board meetings, 10,000 dollars; and the substance record itself, kept by the manager. Total about 95,000 dollars a year, or 475,000 dollars over five years.

A second worked example. With real substance, your adviser now puts the chance of losing at 10 to 20 percent. At 15 percent, expected cost of losing is about 92,000 dollars, plus defence costs if challenged, which may be lower because the evidence is clear; keep 80,000 dollars to be safe. Expected cost about 172,000 dollars, plus 475,000 dollars of substance, about 647,000 dollars, against a saving of 500,000 dollars. On these numbers the structure loses money once it is done properly. That is the most valuable conclusion this lesson can give you: a benefit that only exists while substance is thin is not a benefit.

When substance is cheap insurance

Change one input. Suppose the holding company holds five projects instead of one, saving 500,000 dollars a year rather than 100,000. Substance costs barely change, perhaps 120,000 dollars a year. Over five years the saving is 2,500,000 dollars against 600,000 dollars of substance and a small expected cost of challenge. Now substance is cheap insurance on a large benefit. The same structure that was wrong for one project is right for a portfolio. Scale decides, which is why Warrick warned last week that friction is a fixed cost.

How the best do it

Well-governed international groups treat the substance of each holding entity as a running cost of the structure, budgeted every year, not as an annoyance. They fix a board calendar a year ahead, send papers that contain analysis and options, record dissent and decisions in the minutes, and review residence and permanent establishment risk at least annually with their tax advisers. A small developer can copy the calendar, the papers and the annual review at almost no cost, and can price the rest as this lesson does before forming the entity.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note. An unresolved tax position is a contingent liability on your personal balance sheet if it could flow back to you, for example through guarantees, through clawback of distributions or through your own residence. Carry it at an expected cost, not at zero, and keep enough liquidity to pay the bad case without a forced sale. This is conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Running the sensitivity

The probability of losing drives everything, so do not hide behind a single figure. Run the weak-substance case at both ends of the adviser's range. At 50 percent, expected cost is 305,000 dollars plus 80,000 dollars of defence, 385,000 dollars, leaving a value of about 115,000 dollars. At 70 percent, it is 427,000 dollars plus 80,000 dollars, 507,000 dollars, a loss of about 7,000 dollars. So on weak substance the structure is worth somewhere between a small gain and a small loss, before its running costs, which turn even the best end into a loss. That spread is the honest answer.

Run the severe case as well. Losing in full means 610,000 dollars plus 80,000 dollars of defence, 690,000 dollars, payable in one year, perhaps several years after the dividends were spent. A lender cares about that number more than the expected one, because it decides whether the borrower can still pay debt service in the year the bill arrives. If you cannot fund the severe case from reserves outside the project, the structure is a risk to the project as well as to you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is valuing a structure on its full saving while ignoring the probability that it fails. The control is to price every material tax position as an expected cost with a range, and to keep a structure only if it still pays after the cost of making it real.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner asks the adviser "does this work?" and hears yes. The better question is "what is the probability it is challenged and lost, on our actual facts, and what would change that?"

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught base, downside and severe cases and expected outcomes. A tax position is the same exercise: a probability-weighted cost, a severe case you must survive, and a reserve sized to it.

Recap

Price a residence challenge as tax at stake plus interest and penalties, times the probability of losing, plus defence costs. Price real substance as a yearly running cost. Compare both with the saving. For one small project, substance may cost more than the structure saves; for a portfolio, it is cheap insurance.

Next: Elias, on The Rules: residence tests, permanent establishment and how treaties settle the cases where two countries both claim a taxpayer.
checklist: I price every material tax position as an expected cost with a range.
I include interest, penalties and defence costs, not only the tax.
I ask my adviser for the probability of losing on our actual facts.
I have a yearly budget for the substance of each foreign entity.
I compare the saving with the full cost of making it real.
I reassess a structure's value whenever the number of projects it holds changes.
I carry unresolved tax positions on my balance sheet at expected cost.
head: Field checklist
speak: A tax position is a risk with a price. The expected cost of a residence challenge is the tax at stake, plus interest and penalties, times the probability of losing, plus the cost of defending. In a hypothetical example, a holding company saving 100 thousand dollars a year for five years, on weak substance with a 60 percent chance of losing, has an expected cost of about 446 thousand, so the 500 thousand saving is worth almost nothing. Real substance, meaning resident directors, a small office, a manager who prepares board papers and quarterly meetings, might cost 95 thousand a year and cut the chance of losing to about 15 percent, but then the structure costs more than it saves. For a portfolio of five projects the same substance is cheap insurance. The lesson: a benefit that exists only while substance is thin is not a benefit, and scale decides.
terms: Expected cost — the probability-weighted cost of an uncertain outcome, plus the costs incurred whatever happens.
Penalty — an additional charge imposed for an incorrect tax position, often reduced or avoided where reasonable care was taken.
Defence cost — the advisers' fees, time and attention spent contesting a challenge, paid whether it is won or lost.

hostile.q: Your structure depends on a foreign holding company qualifying. If it is reassessed, where does the cash come from?
hostile.a: I have priced it. The expected cost of a challenge, on our facts and with real substance in place, is about 172 thousand over five years, and the severe case, losing in full, is about 610 thousand plus defence. That severe case is held as a reserve at the holding company level, outside the project's debt service, and it is disclosed to you now. The project's cash flow does not depend on the benefit; it is an upside to equity.

title: The Rules of Residence: Companies, Individuals, Tie-Breakers and Permanent Establishment
summary: Residence rules decide which country may tax a person on worldwide income, and permanent establishment rules decide when a non-resident is taxed on business profits. This lesson sets out the general tests for companies and individuals, how treaties resolve dual residence, and what documentation the rules assume you keep, all as concepts to verify locally.
body:
Residence rules decide who may tax your whole income; permanent establishment rules decide who may tax a slice of it. Know the tests in concept, then verify the exact wording in each country's law and treaty before you rely on any of them.

Recall

Q. How do you price a residence challenge?

A. Tax at stake plus interest and penalties, multiplied by the probability of losing, plus the cost of defending.

Q. What is earned value?

A. The budgeted cost of the work actually completed to date, compared with planned value and actual cost to measure performance.

Q. What does an approval matrix do?

A. It sets who may approve which decisions, by money band and by type of risk, so decisions sit where the risk sits.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, residence is the gateway question in international tax. Get it wrong and every other calculation in the structure is built on the wrong country. Nothing here states the law of any particular country. Residence tests, day counts, treaty thresholds and documentation duties vary and change; verify each point against the primary source before you rely on it, and have it confirmed by a tax adviser licensed in that country.

Companies: three common approaches

In plain English: countries use one or more of three ways to decide where a company lives.

The professional framing. The incorporation test: resident where formed. The central management and control test, from the common law: resident where the board makes the high-level strategic decisions. And a place of effective management test, used in many treaties and some domestic laws: broadly, where the key management and commercial decisions needed for the business as a whole are in substance made. These tests overlap but are not identical, and a company can pass more than one in different countries. Some countries also deem a company formed abroad to be resident if it is managed locally, or treat a locally formed company as non-resident if a treaty assigns its residence elsewhere [unverified — confirm independently].

Individuals: ties, not just days

Your own residence matters too, because a foreign entity you control can be pulled toward wherever you live. Individuals are typically tested by a mix of factors: where you have a home available, where your spouse or dependants live, where your economic and personal ties are, and how many days you spend in the country. Many countries have a day-count rule that makes you resident if you exceed a threshold in a year, but day counts are rarely the only test. For a shift worker who travels, the practical point is to keep a travel log and to know which ties each country weighs. Every threshold and test should be checked in the current law of each country.

Say that out loud now.

Residence is decided by tests and ties; I know the tests in concept and verify the wording in each country.

Tie-breakers in treaties

When two countries both treat a person as resident, a tax treaty between them usually contains a tie-breaker. For individuals, model treaties commonly use a sequence: permanent home, then centre of vital interests, then habitual abode, then nationality, then agreement between the tax authorities. For companies, older treaties often assign residence to the place of effective management; the 2017 update of the OECD model moved toward having the authorities agree case by case, considering factors such as place of effective management, place of incorporation and other relevant factors [unverified — confirm independently]. Which version applies depends on the specific treaty and any later amending instrument. Week 57 takes treaties in depth.

A worked example, hypothetical. A company formed in Country B is managed from Country A. Country B treats it as resident by incorporation; Country A treats it as resident by management. If the A–B treaty uses place of effective management as the tie-breaker, and the effective management is in A, the treaty may assign residence to A, and the company loses Country B's treaty benefits with third countries. If the treaty requires the authorities to agree, the company may face years of uncertainty, and some treaties deny benefits until agreement is reached.

Permanent establishment: the definitions that bite

Most treaties define a permanent establishment as a fixed place of business through which business is carried on, with a list of examples such as a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory or a workshop. They usually add a construction or installation project that lasts longer than a stated period, a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts or plays the principal role in concluding them, and exclusions for preparatory or auxiliary activities such as storage or information gathering. Many treaties have been amended in recent years to tighten agent and anti-fragmentation rules [unverified — confirm independently].

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your company, resident in Country A, sends a project director to Country C for a 14-month build. The A–C treaty sets a construction threshold of 12 months. The site creates a permanent establishment, and Country C may tax the profit attributable to it. If instead the treaty threshold were 18 months, it might not, unless the project director also negotiated and signed contracts locally in a way that made him a dependent agent. Two different tests, either of which can create the presence.

What the rules assume you keep

Residence and PE rules are applied after the fact, on documents. They assume you can show board minutes and attendance, where directors were, who negotiated and signed contracts, how long each site lasted from mobilisation to handover, and travel days for key people. Many countries also require disclosure of foreign entities and treaty-based positions on returns, with penalties for failing to report. Keep the record as you go.

Individuals who travel for work

A worked example, hypothetical and general. A reliability coordinator on a rotating shift lives in Country A with his family, owns his home there, and spends three months a year in Country B supervising a project. Most tests would keep his residence in Country A: his permanent home, his family and his economic ties are there. But his presence in Country B matters for a different question: whether his work there creates a permanent establishment for his company, and whether Country B can tax his own employment income for the days he works there under its domestic law and the treaty. Two separate questions, two different tests, one travel log that answers both.

Keep the log in a simple table: date, country, where you slept, what work you did and who you met. It costs minutes a week. Reconstructing it from bank statements and phone records years later costs days, and it is never as convincing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relying on one test, usually incorporation, when the countries involved apply several. The control is a residence and PE memo for each entity and project, updated yearly, listing every test that could apply and the evidence for each.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts days and stops. Days are one factor among ties, management and agency. Count them, and keep reading.

Callback

In Week 19, LEX taught how law works: statutes, cases and how courts interpret. Residence is a clear example: the statute may say little, and the test lives in cases like De Beers and Fundy and in treaty wording.

Recap

Companies may be resident by incorporation, central management and control, or place of effective management. Individuals are tested by ties and days. Treaties break ties using set sequences or authority agreement. Permanent establishments arise from fixed places, long construction sites and dependent agents. Keep a residence and PE memo for every entity and project.

Professional sign-off required: international tax adviser licensed in each country.

Next: Elias, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a reassessment back to the facts that caused it.
checklist: I know which residence tests each country in my structure applies.
I keep a travel log for myself and every key person.
I have read the tie-breaker clause in each relevant treaty.
I know the construction PE threshold in each treaty where I build.
I know who negotiates and signs contracts in each country.
I keep a residence and PE memo for every entity and project, updated yearly.
I report foreign entities and treaty positions as each country requires.
head: Field checklist
speak: Residence rules decide who may tax your worldwide income; permanent establishment rules decide who may tax a slice of business profit. Companies may be resident by incorporation, by central management and control, or by place of effective management, and a company can pass different tests in different countries. Individuals are tested by ties, such as a home, family and economic interests, and often by day counts, which are rarely the only test. When two countries both claim a person, treaties use tie-breakers: for individuals a sequence beginning with permanent home; for companies, either place of effective management or agreement between the authorities, depending on the treaty. A permanent establishment can arise from a fixed place of business, a construction site lasting longer than the treaty's threshold, or a dependent agent who concludes contracts. All of it is decided on documents, so I keep a residence and PE memo for each entity and project, and verify every test locally.
terms: Place of effective management — broadly, where the key management and commercial decisions needed to run a business as a whole are in substance made.
Tie-breaker — a treaty rule that assigns residence to one country when both domestic laws treat a person as resident.
Dependent agent — a person who habitually concludes contracts, or plays the principal role in concluding them, on behalf of a non-resident business.

hostile.q: Your project director has been in our country for 14 months negotiating with suppliers. Why isn't your company taxable here?
hostile.a: It may well be, and I have planned for that. The site exceeds the treaty's construction threshold, so we have treated it as a permanent establishment from the start, registered as required, and our pro forma carries the tax on the profit attributable to the project. The director's travel days and the contracts he signed are recorded in our residence and PE memo, which we can provide.

title: Reverse Engineering a Reassessment: From the Bill Back to the Facts
summary: This lesson starts from a finished outcome: a hypothetical reassessment treating a foreign holding company as resident at home and a construction site as a permanent establishment. Working backward, it rebuilds the bill, identifies the facts that created each part, and prices what different conduct would have cost.
body:
A reassessment is the end of a story that was written in emails, calendars and site diaries years earlier. Read the bill backward, line by line, to the facts that caused it, and you learn which habits to change before the next one.

Recall

Q. What tie-breaker do model treaties commonly use first for individuals?

A. Where the person has a permanent home available, followed by centre of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality, and then agreement between the authorities.

Q. What is a decision log?

A. The owner's record of each decision: date, decision, who made it, what it cost and what evidence they saw.

Q. What is float in a schedule?

A. The time an activity can slip without delaying the project finish. Who owns it, owner or contractor, is a contract question.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even-numbered week, so we reverse engineer. Every number below is hypothetical, and every rate is invented to show the method, not to describe any country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The value is not the arithmetic. It is seeing that each line of a tax bill traces to a habit that could have been different.

The finished outcome

A developer resident in Country A owns HoldCo, formed in Country B. HoldCo owns ProjectCo in Country C, which built and sold a building. Five years later Country A's authority issues a reassessment with two parts. First, HoldCo is treated as resident in Country A for three years, so dividends it received and a gain it realised are taxed in A. Second, separately, Country C treats the developer's own management company as having had a permanent establishment at the site. The combined bill, hypothetical, is 1,180,000 dollars.

Step 1: split the bill by cause

Ask for the computation, and split it. Residence of HoldCo: dividends of 2,000,000 dollars over three years and a gain of 1,000,000 dollars, taxed in A at a hypothetical 25 percent, gives 750,000 dollars, less a credit for 100,000 dollars of tax already paid in B, so 650,000 dollars. Interest to date, 120,000 dollars. Penalty, hypothetical 10 percent of the tax, 65,000 dollars. Residence subtotal: 835,000 dollars.

The PE in Country C: the management company earned fees of 1,500,000 dollars attributable to site management. Country C attributes 15 percent of that as profit, 225,000 dollars, and taxes it at a hypothetical 30 percent, 67,500 dollars. Add interest of 15,000 dollars. And a late-registration penalty for not registering the PE, hypothetical 262,500 dollars. PE subtotal: 345,000 dollars. Total: 835,000 plus 345,000, which is 1,180,000 dollars. The split already tells you something: the PE tax itself was small, and the penalty for not registering was nearly four times the tax.

Say that out loud now.

Split the bill by cause, then trace each cause to a habit.

Step 2: trace the residence part to the facts

The authority's file shows why it concluded HoldCo was managed in A. Twelve board meetings over three years, all approving resolutions drafted in A and emailed to B the day before. Every significant decision, two land purchases, a loan and four dividends, matched an email from the developer giving the instruction. The directors in B never asked a question recorded in the minutes. Reverse engineered, the residence part of the bill is the price of one habit: sending instructions instead of options.

Step 3: trace the PE part to the facts

The site diary shows mobilisation in month 1 and handover in month 15, 15 months on site, against a treaty construction threshold assumed here at 12 months. The management company's project director signed subcontracts locally. Either fact alone could have created a PE. The tax was predictable from the schedule in month 1. The penalty came from not registering, which is a compliance failure, not a tax planning question.

Step 4: price the alternative conduct

Now work forward from the same facts with different habits, hypothetical costs. Real substance in HoldCo for three years, resident directors who decide, papers with options and a manager in B: about 95,000 dollars a year, 285,000 dollars. With that, the residence challenge is less likely, but price a residual 15 percent chance of the 835,000 dollar outcome, about 125,000 dollars. Expected total: about 410,000 dollars against the actual 835,000 dollars.

For the PE: registering at mobilisation and filing on time, assume compliance costs of 25,000 dollars. The tax of 67,500 dollars would have been paid anyway, without interest or the large penalty. Expected total: about 92,500 dollars against 345,000 dollars. Combined, better habits cost about 502,500 dollars in expectation against the 1,180,000 dollar bill, a difference of about 677,500 dollars. Most of that difference was not clever planning. It was board papers with options, and a registration filed on time.

The table

CauseActual billWith better habits, expectedHabit that changes it
HoldCo residence835,000410,000Options, not instructions; real directors
Site PE345,00092,500Check threshold at mobilisation; register on time
Total1,180,000502,500

Step 5: what the authority could not prove

Reverse engineering also shows what the authority did not have, which is where your adviser builds the response. Here, suppose there were four board meetings in the third year where the papers were drafted by a manager in Country B and contained options, and one where the board declined the developer's proposal. Those meetings are evidence of management in B for at least that year. The reassessment covered three years as if conduct had been uniform. An adviser might argue the third year should fall away, which would remove a share of the residence tax. Whether that argument succeeds depends on local law and the evidence, but it exists only because the record existed.

That is the deeper lesson of the method. A substance record does not only prevent a challenge; it narrows one. Each year in which the record shows real decisions made in the right place is a year an authority must prove otherwise, against documents.

Step 6: the next project's checklist

Turn the table into three lines on the next project's first-day checklist. One: draft every holding company board paper in the country of residence, with options, and minute the discussion. Two: check the construction schedule against every relevant treaty threshold before mobilisation, and register where it is likely to be exceeded. Three: keep the residence and PE memo current every quarter. Three habits, priced against a bill of more than a million dollars.

One more reading of the table is worth saying aloud to your partners. The residence line is a judgment about conduct over years, so it is slow to arise and slow to fix. The PE line is mostly a calendar fact, visible on the first day of the schedule. Put the calendar fact on the project checklist so it can never be missed, and put the conduct question on every board agenda so it is answered a little better each quarter. One is a date to check; the other is a habit to keep.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a reassessment as bad luck rather than as a readout of your habits. The control is to split every tax bill by cause, trace each cause to the documents an authority relied on, and change the habit before the next project.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner fights the tax and ignores the penalty. Here the penalty for not registering was the largest single PE line, and it was entirely avoidable.

Callback

In Week 54, Quincy reverse engineered a cost overrun back to the controls that failed. Today's method is the same: start from the final number, split it by cause, and put a habit beside each cause. A tax bill is a final account for your governance.

Recap

Start from the reassessment, split it into residence and PE, separate tax, interest and penalties, and trace each part to the facts the authority relied on. Price the alternative habits forward. Most of the difference usually comes from board papers that offer options and compliance filed on time.

Professional sign-off required: international tax adviser to review any reassessment and its computation.

Next: Cole, in The Room: a tax authority interview about where decisions were really made.
checklist: I ask for the computation behind any reassessment and split it by cause.
I separate tax, interest and penalties in every bill.
I can trace each part of a bill to the documents an authority relied on.
I check the construction PE threshold against the schedule at mobilisation.
I register for tax where a PE is likely, on time.
I price alternative habits forward before deciding how to respond.
I change the habit before the next project, not just the adviser.
head: Field checklist
speak: A reassessment is the end of a story written years earlier. I read it backward. In a hypothetical example, a 1.18 million dollar bill splits into two causes. The holding company was treated as resident at home because every board decision matched an email I had sent the day before, which with interest and a penalty cost about 835 thousand. Separately, a 15-month site exceeded a 12-month treaty threshold, creating a permanent establishment: the tax was only 67,500, but the penalty for not registering was nearly four times that. Then I price better habits forward: real substance in the holding company and a residual chance of challenge is about 410 thousand in expectation; registering the site on time, about 92,500. Together about half a million against 1.18 million. Most of the difference was not clever planning. It was board papers with options, and a registration filed on time.
terms: Reassessment — a revised tax assessment issued by an authority after reviewing a return, often with interest and penalties.
Computation — the authority's detailed calculation behind a reassessment, which shows the basis for each amount.
Mobilisation — the start of work on a site, from which the duration of a construction project is usually measured.

hostile.q: Your company paid a large PE penalty last year. Why should we trust your compliance on this project?
hostile.a: Because I traced that penalty to its cause and changed the habit. The tax itself was small; the penalty came from not registering a site that ran past the treaty threshold. On this project the schedule was checked against the threshold before mobilisation, we registered in the first month, and the residence and PE memo is updated quarterly. I can show you the registration and the memo now.

title: The Tax Authority Interview: Where Were the Decisions Really Made?
summary: A tax authority reviewing residence will often ask to interview the people involved. This scene follows a composite interview about where a foreign holding company was managed: the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question, when to stay silent, and how to hold your state while being examined.
body:
In a residence interview, the authority already has your emails and minutes. Your job is not to persuade; it is to be accurate, consistent with the documents, brief, and accompanied by your adviser.

Recall

Q. In the Day 5 reassessment, what was the largest single line in the PE part of the bill?

A. The penalty for not registering the permanent establishment, which was nearly four times the tax itself.

Q. What is the first agenda item in a monthly project review?

A. Safety, because it shows the room a guardrail outranks a schedule, and a near miss is evidence a control failed.

Q. What is a baseline?

A. The approved scope, budget and schedule frozen at a date, against which progress is measured.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, an interview with a tax authority is not a negotiation and not a conversation between friends. What you say may be recorded and relied on. The rules on interviews, your rights and whether you must attend differ by country, so take advice before you agree to any interview, and attend with your tax adviser or lawyer. Professional sign-off required: tax lawyer, before and during the interview. The scene below is a composite with hypothetical facts.

The setup

Your holding company, formed in Country B, has been resident there for four years, and you live in Country A. Country A's authority is reviewing whether it is really managed in A. You have agreed, on your lawyer's advice, to a voluntary interview. In the room: two officers, your lawyer, and you. Your lawyer has prepared you: answer the question asked, from your own knowledge, refer to documents, and say when you do not know.

The opening

The officer asks you to describe your role in the holding company. Say: "I am its sole shareholder. I am not a director. The board of two directors in Country B makes its decisions. I propose matters to the board as a shareholder, usually in writing, and it decides. The board papers and minutes are in the bundle my lawyer provided."

That answer states a role, not an argument. It also commits you to a position that must match every document they hold. If it would not, the time to correct the facts was before the interview, with your lawyer, not in it.

The questions, and the question behind each

The officer asks: "Did you ever tell the directors what to decide?" The question behind it is: "Will your answer match the emails we have?" Answer truthfully. If there was a period when you did give instructions, say so and say what changed: "In the first year I sent instructions. My advisers told me that was wrong, and from the second year the board received papers with options. You will see that in the minutes." A consistent, honest account of a corrected practice is far better than a denial an email contradicts.

The officer asks: "Has the board ever refused something you proposed?" The question behind it is: "Is the board real?" If it has, refer to the minute: "Yes, in the third year it declined a loan to another of my companies until it had an independent valuation. Minute 14 records it." Then stop. Do not add colour.

The officer asks: "Where were you when the board approved the land purchase?" The question behind it is: "Were you present, by phone or in person, and did you lead?" Say what you know, and if you do not remember, say: "I don't recall. My travel log for that date is in the bundle." Never guess a date or a place.

Say that out loud now.

Answer the question asked, from my own knowledge, point to the document, and stop.

Lines never to say

Never say "the company is in Country B for tax reasons". It invites the conclusion that it has no other purpose. Never speculate about what the directors were thinking; they can speak for themselves. Never volunteer documents or facts you have not reviewed with your lawyer. Never say "everyone structures it this way". And never answer a question you do not understand; ask for it to be repeated or rephrased.

When to stay silent

Officers sometimes leave silence after an answer, and the instinct is to fill it with more explanation. Do not. A complete answer followed by silence is still complete. If your lawyer asks for a break, take it. If a question strays into areas you have not prepared, your lawyer may ask that it be put in writing; let your lawyer handle that.

Holding your state

You will feel defensive, because the questions imply you did something wrong. Slow your speech. Keep your answers short. Treat each question as a request for one fact. If you notice your heart rate rising, pause before answering; a pause is normal and reads as care. If you use a breathing routine to settle before the meeting, do it parked or seated, never while driving, and check with your doctor if you have any health condition.

A worked example of a good and a bad answer

Question: "Who decided the dividend of 400,000 dollars in year three?" Bad answer: "Well, obviously the board, though I suppose I suggested a number, because I know the projects best, and they generally go along with what makes sense." Every clause of that answer helps the authority's case. Good answer: "The board, at its June meeting. I wrote to it as shareholder in May proposing 500,000 dollars. The board set 400,000 dollars to keep a reserve. Both documents are in the bundle." One version describes a puppet; the other describes a board.

A second example: "Do you consider yourself to control the company?" Good answer: "I own all its shares, so I can appoint and remove directors as shareholder. The directors manage it." That is accurate, and it separates ownership from management, which is the distinction residence turns on.

After the interview

As soon as the interview ends, sit with your lawyer and write down, while memory is fresh, every question asked, every answer you gave and every document referred to. If you realise an answer was wrong or incomplete, tell your lawyer immediately; a prompt correction in writing is far better than leaving an inaccuracy on the record. Do not contact the officers yourself afterwards. Do not discuss the interview with the directors until your lawyer has advised whether and how to do so, because coordinating accounts, or appearing to, can damage the credibility of everyone involved.

Then add a note to your decision journal: what the authority focused on, which documents carried weight and which habits in your own governance you would change. The interview is expensive training. Do not waste it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an answer that is inconsistent with the documents, which damages your credibility on every other point. The control is preparation with your lawyer against the full document bundle, and a commitment to answer only from your own knowledge.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to win the interview by explaining the whole structure and its logic. The interview is for facts. The argument belongs to your lawyer, in writing, later.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught acknowledge, bridge, answer for hostile questions. In a tax interview, drop the bridge. Acknowledge the question, answer it from the documents, and stop; bridging to a message sounds like advocacy, and advocacy is your lawyer's job.

Recap

Take advice before any interview and attend with your lawyer. State your role, answer only what is asked, from your own knowledge, refer to documents, and stop. Admit and explain corrected practices rather than deny them. Never speculate, never volunteer unreviewed material, and never describe an entity as existing for tax.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap, with Cole's Auditor's Chair on a set of board minutes.
checklist: I take legal advice before agreeing to any tax interview.
I attend every interview with my tax lawyer.
I review the full document bundle before the interview.
I answer only the question asked, from my own knowledge.
I admit and explain any corrected practice rather than deny it.
I never guess dates, places or other people's thinking.
I never describe an entity as existing for tax reasons.
head: Field checklist
speak: In a residence interview the authority already has my emails and minutes, so my job is accuracy, consistency and brevity, with my lawyer beside me. I take advice before agreeing to attend. I state my role plainly: sole shareholder, not a director; the board decides. When asked whether I ever told the directors what to decide, I tell the truth, and if there was an early period of instructions, I say so and point to when the practice changed. When asked whether the board ever refused me, I cite the minute and stop. If I do not remember where I was, I say so and point to my travel log. I never say the entity exists for tax reasons, never speculate about what the directors thought, and never volunteer unreviewed documents. I keep answers short, pause before answering, and leave the argument to my lawyer, in writing, later.
terms: Document bundle — the organised set of documents provided to an authority or prepared for an interview, which answers should match.
Voluntary interview — an interview a taxpayer agrees to attend, whose rules and rights depend on local law.
Ownership versus management — the distinction between the shareholder who owns and appoints, and the board that manages and decides.

hostile.q: You own every share of this company and you proposed every dividend. Why isn't it managed by you?
hostile.a: I own it, and as shareholder I can appoint and remove the directors. The directors manage it. I propose matters in writing, as the minutes show, and the board decides; it has set different dividends from those I proposed and declined at least one transaction I wanted until it had independent evidence. My lawyer has provided the minutes and papers, and the directors can speak to their own decisions.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 56 Review: Residence and Substance
summary: This review tests the week: residence by incorporation or by management, permanent establishment, the substance record, pricing a challenge, treaty tie-breakers and the interview. Because this is a fourth week, the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair, reading a set of hypothetical board minutes as a hostile auditor would.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: an entity lives where it is really run and is taxed where its work is really done, and the only proof is a record kept as it happens.

Recall

Q. In a tax interview, what should you do after a complete answer?

A. Stop talking. Silence after a complete answer is still a complete answer; the argument belongs to your lawyer, in writing.

Q. What is Rule 55?

A. Every entity has a one-sentence business purpose, every related-party arrangement is disclosed and independently priced, and the whole structure is drawn on one page for any lender or investor before they commit.

Q. What is an owner decision log?

A. The record of each decision: date, decision, who made it, what it cost and the evidence seen.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, residence and substance sit underneath every treaty benefit and every repatriation plan in the weeks ahead. If you can answer these six questions without notes, Week 57 on treaties will make sense. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the two broad tests of company residence?

Answer: Incorporation, resident where formed; and management, resident where central management and control is actually exercised, meaning where the board makes the high-level decisions. Many treaties also use place of effective management.

Question 2. What is a permanent establishment, and how can a construction project create one?

Answer: A fixed place of business or dependent agent through which a business becomes taxable in a country under a treaty. A construction site lasting longer than the treaty's stated period usually creates one.

Question 3. What goes in a substance record?

Answer: Board calendars and attendance, minutes with the papers actually considered, where directors were when they decided, the entity's own office, staff and bank mandate, and travel logs for key people, all kept as events happen.

Question 4. How do you price a residence challenge?

Answer: Tax at stake plus interest and penalties, multiplied by the probability of losing, plus defence costs, then compare that with the saving and the cost of real substance.

Question 5. What do treaty tie-breakers do?

Answer: They assign residence to one country when both treat a person as resident, using a sequence for individuals, and for companies either place of effective management or agreement between the authorities, depending on the treaty.

Question 6. What did Fundy teach you?

Answer: Rule 56: an entity I set up abroad must be governed there in fact; if I keep the real decisions, I treat it as resident where I live.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Elias framed residence by management and taxation where work is done. Ford and Cole took the Fundy Settlement case, giving Rule 56. Roman priced a residence challenge against the cost of real substance. Elias set out residence tests, tie-breakers and permanent establishment definitions. Elias reverse engineered a reassessment back to the habits that caused it. Cole ran a tax authority interview.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 56 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read these hypothetical board minutes as a hostile tax auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Minutes of the Board of HoldCo Limited, held by telephone. Present: Director A, Director B. In attendance: the Shareholder. 1. The Board noted the Shareholder's instruction dated 3 March and resolved accordingly to acquire the shares of LandCo for 2,000,000 dollars. 2. The Board approved the dividend proposed by the Shareholder. 3. The Board approved a loan of 500,000 dollars to DevCo, a company owned by the Shareholder, interest-free. 4. There being no further business, the meeting closed after ten minutes. Signed: Director A.

The defects. First, the meeting was held by telephone, with no record of where the directors were, so the minutes cannot show the decisions were made in the country of residence. Second, the shareholder was in attendance and the board "noted the Shareholder's instruction and resolved accordingly", an admission that the decision was made elsewhere. Third, the dividend was approved as proposed, with no amount, no analysis of reserves and no recorded discussion. Fourth, an interest-free loan to a company owned by the shareholder is a related-party transaction with no evidence of arm's-length terms, which invites both a transfer pricing and a governance challenge. Fifth, three significant decisions in ten minutes suggests ratification, not management. Sixth, no papers are listed as considered. Seventh, the minutes are signed by one director with no date.

Then the auditor asks for evidence: the email of 3 March, the directors' travel records for the meeting date, any analysis behind the price paid for LandCo, the dividend calculation, the loan agreement and any valuation. If those documents show the decisions were made by the shareholder in Country A, the minutes have become evidence for the authority, not against it.

A worked rewrite of item 1: "The Board considered a paper from the manager, circulated on 1 March, setting out three options for the LandCo acquisition, an independent valuation of 1,900,000 to 2,100,000 dollars and the Shareholder's proposal. After discussion of financing and risk, the Board resolved to acquire at 2,000,000 dollars. Both directors attended in person at the company's office." That minute describes management.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why does it matter where we hold the board meetings?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because where the decisions are really made can decide which country taxes the company. Many countries treat a company as resident where its central management and control is exercised, so a company formed abroad but run by us from here can be taxed here, and lose the benefit that justified it. That is what happened to the trusts in the Fundy case in Canada in 2012. So the board has to be real: directors who receive options, decide and sometimes say no, meeting where the company is resident, with minutes that show the debate. Separately, a long construction site abroad can create a permanent establishment, so we check the treaty threshold before we mobilise. We price each tax position as an expected cost, budget for substance, and keep the record as we go, because years later the record is all anyone will look at."

Score your answer. Did you lead with the bottom line? Did you name the management test and give one example? Did you mention permanent establishment? Did you finish inside two minutes?

Using the Auditor's Chair on your own board

Take the last three sets of minutes from any entity you control and read them as Cole did. For each significant decision, ask: is there a paper, does it show options, is the discussion recorded, do we know where each director was, and could the board have decided differently? Mark each minute as management or ratification. If most are ratification, the problem is not the minutes; it is how the decisions are made. Fix the process first, and the minutes will follow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is board minutes that describe ratification rather than management. The control is papers with options, real discussion, recorded locations and decisions the directors could have made differently.

The beginner's mistake

Treating minutes as a formality written after the fact. Minutes are evidence, and they are read most carefully by people who were not there.

Callback

In Week 54, Ford took Sampoong, where an owner removed the people paid to say no. A board that never says no is the tax version of the same failure: an approval authority that exists on paper and not in fact.

Recap

Residence by incorporation or management, permanent establishment by place, site or agent, a substance record kept as you go, tax positions priced as expected costs, tie-breakers in treaties, and accurate, brief answers in an interview. Rule 56 keeps foreign entities governed where they claim to live.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was residence and substance. A company may be resident where it was formed or where it is really managed, and the management test looks at where the board makes the high-level decisions. A business can also be taxed where it has a permanent establishment, including a construction site lasting longer than a treaty threshold, or an agent who concludes contracts. Both are decided on evidence, so I keep a substance record as events happen. I price every tax position as an expected cost and compare it with the cost of real substance; for one small project substance can cost more than the saving, for a portfolio it is cheap insurance. Treaties break dual residence with tie-breakers. In an interview I answer accurately, briefly and from documents, with my lawyer. Rule 56, from the Fundy case: a foreign entity must be governed abroad in fact, or I treat it as resident where I live.
terms: Auditor's Chair — reading a document as a hostile auditor would, to find what it reveals against its author.
Ratification — formally approving a decision already made elsewhere, as opposed to making it.
Board paper — a document circulated before a meeting setting out the facts, options and analysis the directors will decide on.

hostile.q: Your board minutes are signed and approved. Why should I treat them as evidence of real management?
hostile.a: You should not on signatures alone, and I would not ask you to. Read them with the papers: each significant decision has a paper circulated in advance with options and independent evidence, the discussion is recorded, the directors attended in person at the company's office, and on two occasions the board decided differently from what I proposed as shareholder. The travel logs and the papers are in the bundle, and they match the minutes.
